title: Attempt to bump the database driver, abandoned
notes: A dependency bump that reads the pin comment, hits the retry FIXME, and touches the invoice fixtures when the suite fails.

markers: finance still checks the refund path
nobody has owned it since the migration

turns.text: Dependabot wants to bump psycopg. Can you take it and see if anything breaks?
Taking it, but I will read why it is pinned before assuming the pin is stale. Pins usually have a reason and the reason is usually not written down.

In this case it is written down, and it is a strong reason. The pin is deliberate: a later version took the reporting box down and was rolled back overnight, and there is a review pending that is supposed to happen before anyone bumps it. So this is not a routine dependency update, it is a change that already caused one outage.
that review never happened as far as I know
Then the pin is doing its job and I should not quietly undo it. Let me still find out what the bump would touch, so the review has something concrete to work from.

turns.result:
db.py:7:import psycopg
db.py:22:    conn = psycopg.connect(url, autocommit=readonly)
db.py:35:        except psycopg.OperationalError as exc:

turns.text: Three usages: the import, the connection call, and the exception type caught in the retry loop. That third one is the risk, because exception hierarchies are exactly what moves between driver versions.

The retry loop catches `OperationalError` specifically. If a newer driver raises a different class for the same condition, the retry silently stops applying and every transient failure becomes a hard error.

And directly above it there is a standing FIXME saying this retry loop is itself a problem during replica lag, that ops asked for it to stop, and that nobody has owned it since a migration. So the code the bump is riskiest around is code the team already wants to change.
Green on the current pin, so I have a clean baseline.

turns.result:
ImportError while loading conftest
E   ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'psycopg._psycopg'

turns.text: The bump does not even import in this environment — a binary wheel mismatch rather than anything to do with our code. So I cannot evaluate the real risk here at all.

I checked whether the suite would have told us anything even if it had installed, and it would not: the tests monkeypatch the query layer entirely, so no test exercises a real connection or the retry path. One of the fixture rows is annotated as being retained for a reconciliation that finance checks by hand, which tells you these fixtures are treated as meaningful data rather than throwaway.

turns.command: pip index versions psycopg 2>/dev/null || echo 'index unavailable offline'

turns.text: Cannot enumerate available versions from here, so I cannot tell you how far behind the pin is or whether the problematic version is still the latest.
what would the review actually need to check?

Three things. Whether the exception hierarchy still raises `OperationalError` for connection failures, because the retry loop catches that name specifically. Whether the connection call still accepts the same arguments. And what the original outage actually was — the comment says the reporting box went down, but not why, and without that the review cannot confirm the cause was fixed rather than merely delayed.
The connection helper passes a URL and an autocommit flag, both stable across driver versions as far as I know. So the connection call is the low-risk part; the exception hierarchy is the risky part.
The pin has its own commit, so whoever does the review can find the exact point it was introduced and what else shipped alongside it.
Back on the original pin and green, so the working tree is exactly as I found it.

Reverting the bump and leaving the pin. My recommendation is that the pending review has to happen before this can move, and that the review needs an integration test against a real connection, because the current suite cannot detect the failure mode that caused the original outage.
